quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten quick checks on relative cover, cover factor and cloth cover as the designer uses them.

questions.q: Relative cover of one thread set is defined as which ratio?
questions.explain: Relative cover is d/p: the fraction of the thread spacing that the yarn diameter fills. p/d is the reverse ratio and would be greater than 1 for an open cloth.

questions.q: With density in threads per 100 mm and count in tex, the cover factor K = n√tex has a maximum value of 2,670.
questions.explain: At K = 2,670 the diameter √tex ÷ 26.7 exactly equals the spacing 100 ÷ n, so d/p = 1 and the threads touch. Any larger value would mean yarns thicker than the space available.

questions.q: What does the number 2,670 in the lecture represent?
options: The constant that converts tex to Ne
The maximum cloth cover of warp and weft together
The threads per 100 mm of a square cloth
The value of K at which yarn diameter equals thread spacing (full cover)
questions.explain: 2,670 is 26.7 × 100: the cover factor at which d/p = 1. It is not a density and has nothing to do with the tex–Ne conversion (590.5).

questions.q: In the diameter formula d = √tex ÷ 26.7, in what unit is d given?
questions.explain: The lecture states d = √tex ÷ 26.7 mm; for 25 tex that is 5 ÷ 26.7 = 0.187 mm, which matches the worksheet. Tex is a count, not a length.

questions.q: Cloth cover is found by simply adding the warp cover and the weft cover.
questions.explain: Adding would count the crossings (where warp lies over weft) twice. Cloth cover is C₁ + C₂ − C₁C₂; for 0.50 and 0.75 it is 0.875, not 1.25.

questions.q: Which quantity in the lecture equals 1 − C, where C is the cloth cover?
options: The relative cover of the weft
The open area through which air and light pass
questions.explain: With C = 0.88 the lecture says the remaining 12% is the open area that lets air and light through. Crimp and weavability are separate ideas from Weaving Calculations.

questions.q: The equivalent Ne cover factor used in the worksheet is calculated as
questions.explain: Row 9 of the worksheet is labelled EPI/√Ne: ends per inch divided by the square root of the English cotton count. Multiplying by √Ne would make finer yarns look better covered, the wrong way round.

questions.q: K = n√tex uses threads per 100 mm and tex. The Ne cover factor uses which pair?
questions.explain: The Ne version is the traditional imperial form: ends (or picks) per inch divided by √Ne. Mixing per-inch density with tex, or per-100 mm density with Ne, gives numbers that match neither scale.

questions.q: A relative cover of 0.50 means the yarn diameter is half the spacing between thread centres.
questions.explain: d/p = 0.50 is exactly that: in the lecture's warp, d = 0.187 mm and p = 0.375 mm, so the yarn fills half its space and the other half is gap.

questions.q: Which two things fix the cover factor of one thread set?
questions.explain: K = n√tex needs only the density n and the count in tex. Weave affects how much cover is weavable (Weaving Calculations 12–13) but not the value of K itself.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: How d, p, K and cloth cover respond when count, density or one set's cover is changed.

questions.q: The tex of a yarn is quadrupled while threads per 100 mm stay the same. The cover factor K
questions.explain: K depends on √tex, and √4 = 2, so K doubles. Quadrupling is the tempting answer if you forget the square root.

questions.q: With n threads per 100 mm, the spacing p in millimetres is
questions.explain: 100 mm shared among n threads gives 100 ÷ n mm each: 100 ÷ 267 = 0.375 mm in the lecture. n ÷ 100 would be threads per millimetre, not a spacing.

questions.q: With n in threads per 100 mm and count in tex, relative cover d/p = n√tex ÷ 2,670.
At the same count, the thread density is doubled (still well short of full cover). The relative cover
questions.explain: d/p is proportional to n, so doubling n doubles the cover. The √2 answer confuses density with tex, which enters as a square root.

questions.q: If the warp already covers fully (C₁ = 1), the cloth cover C₁ + C₂ − C₁C₂ equals
questions.explain: 1 + C₂ − 1 × C₂ = 1. Once one set covers everything, the other can add nothing; cloth cover can never exceed 1.

questions.q: Why is the product C₁C₂ subtracted in the cloth cover formula?
options: Because weft yarns are weaker than warp yarns
To allow for the weave structure
Because crimp reduces the effective diameter
Because the area where warp and weft overlap would otherwise be counted twice
questions.explain: C₁ + C₂ double-counts the overlap, whose fraction is C₁C₂ when the sets are independent. The formula does not depend on the weave or on crimp.

questions.q: Because 2,670 is the maximum of K, the relative cover d/p of a weavable thread set never exceeds 1.
questions.explain: d/p = K ÷ 2,670, so K ≤ 2,670 means d/p ≤ 1: the yarns can at most touch. Values above 1 would require yarns wider than their spacing.

questions.q: To convert threads per 100 mm into threads per inch, multiply by
questions.explain: An inch is 25.4 mm, i.e. 0.254 of 100 mm, so 267 per 100 mm = 267 × 0.254 = 67.8 per inch. Multiplying by 2.54 gives threads per 10 mm, ten times too many.

questions.q: The English cotton count Ne is obtained from tex by
questions.explain: Ne is an indirect count, so Ne = 590.5 ÷ tex: 25 tex is Ne 23.6. 1,000 ÷ tex would be metric count Nm.

questions.q: Two cloths both have cloth cover 0.88, one with the higher cover in the warp, the other in the weft. Their open areas are
options: Impossible to compare without the weave
questions.explain: Open area is 1 − C, and both have C = 0.88, so both are 12% open. The formula is symmetrical in warp and weft.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Work through diameters, spacings, cover factors and cloth cover for new thread sets.

questions.q: A warp yarn is 49 tex. Its diameter d = √tex ÷ 26.7, in mm to three decimals?
The warp is set at 240 threads per 100 mm. Thread spacing p in mm, to three decimals?
Cover factor K = n√tex for 49 tex at 240 threads per 100 mm?
Relative cover d/p of that warp (K = 1,680), to three decimals?
The weft is 20 tex at 300 picks per 100 mm. Relative cover of the weft, to two decimals?
Warp cover 0.63 and weft cover 0.50. Cloth cover C₁ + C₂ − C₁C₂, to three decimals?
A cloth has cover 0.815. Its open area as a percentage, to one decimal?
A sample has 72 ends per inch of Ne 16 yarn. Ne cover factor EPI ÷ √Ne?
The lecture's weft is 36 tex at 334 picks per 100 mm. Its cover factor K is
questions.explain: K = 334 × √36 = 334 × 6 = 2,004. 1,335 is the warp's value; 1,202 comes from using 3.6 instead of 6.

questions.q: At what density would 25 tex yarn reach full cover (K = 2,670)?
questions.explain: n = 2,670 ÷ √25 = 2,670 ÷ 5 = 534 threads per 100 mm — exactly twice the lecture's 267, which gave cover 0.50.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Design-office situations: choosing counts and setts, spotting errors in cover calculations.

questions.q: A designer wants more cover from a cloth without changing the yarn count. The direct way is to
options: Use a finer yarn at the same density
questions.explain: At fixed tex, K rises in proportion to n. A finer yarn at the same density lowers K; crimp is not in the formula.

questions.q: A cloth has warp cover 0.95 and weft cover 0.30. Raising weft cover to 0.60 would change cloth cover from about 0.965 to about
questions.explain: 0.95 + 0.60 − 0.57 = 0.98. Because the warp already covers 95%, extra weft adds very little; 1.25 and 1.55 come from adding without subtracting the overlap.

questions.q: For a light, airy summer fabric a low cloth cover is the appropriate design target.
questions.explain: Open area 1 − C is what lets air through; a low cover leaves more open area. Curtains or shade cloth would need the opposite.

questions.q: Fabric A has 30 tex warp at 250 per 100 mm; fabric B has 20 tex warp at 300 per 100 mm. Which warp has the higher cover?
options: Cannot be told without the weave
questions.explain: A: 250 × √30 = 250 × 5.477 = 1,369; B: 300 × √20 = 300 × 4.472 = 1,342. A is slightly higher; the extra density of B does not quite make up for its finer yarn.

questions.q: A mill proposes 40 tex yarn at 350 threads per 100 mm. Cover factor K to the nearest whole number?
A sample card reads 80 EPI, Ne 20. The Ne cover factor is
questions.explain: 80 ÷ √20 = 80 ÷ 4.472 = 17.9. Dividing by 20 gives 4.0 (forgot the root); multiplying by √20 gives 357.8.

questions.q: A trainee computes K with threads per cm instead of threads per 100 mm. The result is
questions.explain: Threads per cm is one tenth of threads per 100 mm, so K and the relative cover come out one tenth of their true values — 0.05 instead of 0.50 for the lecture's warp.

questions.q: A colleague says a cloth with warp cover 0.50 and weft cover 0.75 is '125% covered'. What is wrong?
options: The overlap C₁C₂ = 0.375 has been counted twice; cloth cover is 0.875
The two covers should have been multiplied, giving 0.375
The weft cover should have been ignored
questions.explain: Cloth cover = 0.50 + 0.75 − 0.375 = 0.875, so 12.5% is open. Multiplying alone gives only the overlap area, not the covered area.

questions.q: At the same yarn count, a cloth with a higher cover factor is heavier per square metre.
questions.explain: Same tex and a higher K means more threads per 100 mm, so more yarn in each square metre. Weight also rises if tex rises at fixed density.

questions.q: As K approaches 2,670 for one set, what practical problem does the weaver face?
options: The yarn becomes too fine to spin
Weavability: the threads can no longer be beaten up without weave corrections
questions.explain: The lecture points to Weaving Calculations 12–13 for weavability limits and weave corrections; near full cover the interlacings leave no room for more threads.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Two-step reasoning across the whole lecture: inverting the formulas, comparing options and catching common slips.

questions.q: The lecture cloth has warp cover 0.50 and weft cover 0.75. Adding 0.10 of relative cover to one set only, which gives the larger cloth cover?
options: Both give the same cloth cover
Adding it to the warp (the less covered set)
questions.explain: Warp +0.10: 0.60 + 0.75 − 0.45 = 0.90. Weft +0.10: 0.50 + 0.85 − 0.425 = 0.925. A gain in one set is worth (1 − cover of the other set): the weft's partner, the warp, leaves 0.50 uncovered, the warp's partner only 0.25.

questions.q: Warp cover 0.50, weft cover raised to 0.85. Cloth cover to three decimals?
A target cloth cover of 0.90 is wanted with a warp cover of 0.60. Required weft cover, to two decimals?
A student writes d = 25 ÷ 26.7 = 0.936 mm for a 25 tex yarn. The mistake is
options: Using the wrong constant; it should be 2,670
Forgetting the square root: d = √25 ÷ 26.7 = 0.187 mm
questions.explain: The formula is √tex ÷ 26.7. 0.936 mm would be a yarn five times too thick, giving a relative cover of 2.5 at 267 per 100 mm — clearly impossible.

questions.q: A weft set at 334 picks per 100 mm has K = 2,004. What is its count in tex?
questions.explain: √tex = 2,004 ÷ 334 = 6, so tex = 6² = 36 — the lecture's weft.

questions.q: For the lecture's warp (25 tex, 267 per 100 mm) the Ne cover factor is about 14 and its maximum is about 28, so the ratio to full cover is the same 0.50 as in tex terms.
questions.explain: 267 × 0.254 = 67.8 EPI; Ne = 590.5 ÷ 25 = 23.6, √Ne = 4.86; 67.8 ÷ 4.86 = 14.0. The full-cover value 2,670 converts the same way to about 27.9, so the ratio is still 0.50.

questions.q: Warp and weft each have a relative cover of 0.50. The cloth cover is
questions.explain: 0.50 + 0.50 − 0.25 = 0.75. 1.00 ignores the overlap; 0.25 is only the overlap.

questions.q: 30 tex warp at 280 per 100 mm and 30 tex weft at 220 per 100 mm. Cloth cover to three decimals?
Which change leaves the cloth cover of the lecture's fabric (0.50 warp, 0.75 weft) unchanged?
options: Swapping the two covers so the warp is 0.75 and the weft 0.50
Doubling both yarn counts in tex
questions.explain: C₁ + C₂ − C₁C₂ is symmetrical, so swapping gives the same 0.875. Doubling tex multiplies each cover by √2; changing a density changes that set's cover.

questions.q: A student reports open area = 1 − 0.50 − 0.75 = −0.25 and calls the cloth 'over-covered'. The correct open area is
questions.explain: Cloth cover is 0.875, so open area is 1 − 0.875 = 0.125 = 12.5%. A negative open area is the sign that the overlap was not subtracted.
